prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You

outputs.L1:
You must understand that sighting the pair of eagles over the block, directly above our house, no more than twenty feet above the roof—so massive that their wings seem to tug at the corrugated tin sheeting with even the gentlest tilt—counteracts the bitterness I feel toward all the damage I see and hear around me on an exceptionally crisp blue morning, when clarity itself is pain, and even one small missing wattle tree, entirely vanquished since I was last here at home—I still find this hard to say—is agony.

A region is not a pinpoint, and a different compass works in my head, one with magnetics for all directions, all pointing to one spot I know and observe as closely as possible. Even one small vanished or vanquished wattle tree is agony, close to death for me, where I find it hard to breathe, to feed myself, to move beyond the loss.

But the pair of eagles still appearing, still keeping their sharp and scrupulous eyes honed, overrides this ordeal—though I wish life for their victims too, and their damage is as traumatic as anything else. That is as much sense, or nonsense, as I can make in such blue light.
outputs.L2: You have to grasp that seeing the two eagles above the block, directly over our house, no higher than twenty feet over the roof—their bodies so huge that, with even the softest angle of their wings, they seem to tug at the corrugated tin—balances out the resentment I feel toward all the harm I can see and hear around me on a perfectly sharp blue morning, when such clearness itself hurts and when even a single small wattle tree, gone completely since the last time I was home—I still struggle to put this into words—feels like torment. A region cannot be reduced to a dot, and in my mind some other kind of compass operates, one charged with magnetism in every direction, yet every direction leads back to one place I recognize and watch as carefully as I can. Even one little wattle tree that has disappeared, or been destroyed, is for me a pain almost like death, a place where I can barely breathe, barely eat, barely move beyond the loss. And yet the eagles continue to show themselves, their keen, exacting eyes still sharpened and alert, and their presence rises above this suffering—though I also wish life for whatever they hunt, and the hurt they cause is as shocking as any other harm. That is the nearest I can come to sense, or perhaps nonsense, beneath such blue light.
outputs.L3:
The sight of a pair of eagles flying low over the speaker’s house provides a moment of relief from the bitterness they feel about the damage in the surrounding landscape. Their presence is striking and beautiful, and it briefly lifts the speaker out of grief. This does not erase the destruction, but it counteracts it, offering a powerful image of freedom and vitality.

At the same time, the speaker experiences the loss of even a single wattle tree as deeply painful. The death or removal of one tree is not treated as a small event; instead, it feels almost unbearable. This shows how emotionally attached the speaker is to the natural world around them, and how acutely they register every wound inflicted on it.

The speaker’s connection to this particular place is intense and personal. It is as though their whole inner life is oriented toward it, with every direction in their mind leading back to this landscape. The place is not merely a setting, but a centre of memory, feeling, and identity.

The eagles offer consolation because they embody a kind of wild beauty that still survives. However, this comfort is complicated by the speaker’s awareness that the eagles are predators. Their lives depend on acts of violence and harm to other creatures. As a result, the speaker cannot see them as purely innocent or purely redemptive.

The poem therefore presents a conflicted response to nature. Beauty and loss exist side by side, as do violence and consolation. Beneath the clear blue sky, the speaker finds both pain and relief, recognizing that the natural world is capable of inspiring grief, wonder, bitterness, and comfort all at once.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts ecological loss and personal grief through the speaker’s careful observation of two eagles circling above the home. Rather than presenting nature as distant or untouched, the poem places wildness directly within the speaker’s damaged world. The eagles become a sudden, vivid presence against a background of environmental decline, reminding the speaker of what still survives even as so much has been harmed or lost. Their flight draws the speaker’s attention upward, away from private sorrow and toward a larger, living world that continues to move with grace and power.

At the same time, the poem does not suggest that the sight of the eagles can undo grief or repair ecological destruction. The damage remains real, and the speaker’s awareness of loss is not erased by this moment of beauty. Instead, the eagles offer a temporary interruption of despair. Their presence creates a brief space in which the speaker can feel wonder, connection, and perhaps even hope. This hope is fragile, because it exists alongside the knowledge that the natural world is under threat. Yet the poem values that fragility, suggesting that even a fleeting encounter with wild beauty can matter deeply.

In this way, the eagles serve as both symbols of endurance and reminders of vulnerability. They embody strength, freedom, and majesty, but their appearance also emphasizes how rare and precious such moments have become. The poem’s emotional power comes from this tension: the speaker sees beauty without forgetting devastation, and experiences relief without claiming that everything is healed. Ultimately, the poem suggests that paying close attention to the living world can help resist complete despair. Beauty cannot cancel loss, but it can briefly counter it, offering a moment of consolation amid ecological and personal grief.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single long, breathless free-verse poem about seeing a pair of eagles flying low over a rural house, where the beauty of the sight briefly counteracts grief over environmental damage and a missing wattle tree.
counterfactuals.output:
I was standing by the rural house with its tin roof holding the afternoon heat like an old sorrow,  
the paddocks rubbed thin by drought and machinery and the patient teeth of animals,  
the creek below the fence gone to stones and a few greenish mirrors,  
the wind carrying dust instead of blossom,  
and I was thinking again of the wattle tree that used to burn there in winter,  
yellow as sudden laughter beside the gate,  
the one cut down or dead or simply vanished into the long accounting of what we take and fail to notice taking,  
and I was grieving it in that small helpless way we grieve what cannot answer,  
the bees that should have crowded its gold,  
the birds that should have stitched themselves into its shade,  
the soft rain of pollen on the grass,  
the whole bright architecture of it missing from the air,  
when over the house they came,  
two eagles,  
low, so low the world seemed to duck beneath them,  
their wings wide enough to silence the yard,  
their shadows sliding over the veranda, the water tank, the cracked path,  
and for a moment even the rusted ute and the plastic caught in the fence and the empty place where the wattle had been  
were gathered into something larger than damage,  
not forgiven, no, never that,  
but held,  
as if the sky had lowered its hands to lift the day by the shoulders,  
and the eagles moved without hurry,  
without apology,  
great brown bodies breathing the air into shape,  
feathered wrists flexing,  
eyes turned toward some invisible current rising off the fields,  
and I felt my grief stop mid-sentence,  
not end,  
not heal,  
but pause like a dog hearing a far whistle,  
because beauty had arrived without permission and was crossing the roofline,  
because the ruined world had still produced this double astonishment,  
because above the scarred earth and the absent tree and the shrinking shade and the old human mess of clearing, burning, poisoning, forgetting,  
there were these two living commas in the hot blue sentence of the afternoon,  
and they flew so close I could almost believe they had come to inspect us,  
to see what we had done with the place,  
to measure the loss of the wattle, the thinning creek, the tired soil,  
then to offer, not absolution, not comfort exactly,  
but evidence,  
wingbeat after wingbeat,  
that the earth was not yet only a record of vanishing,  
that something fierce and sovereign still wrote itself across the air,  
and I stood beneath them with my mouth open,  
held between mourning and praise,  
between the stump in memory and the living sky,  
between all that has been felled and all that still rises,  
watching until they slipped beyond the house,  
beyond the paddock,  
beyond the line of trees that remains,  
and the silence came back altered,  
as if the missing wattle had bloomed for one impossible second in the shadows of their wings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an ecopoem in a dense, Australian pastoral style, using corrugated tin, wattle trees, eagles, blue morning light, and the speaker’s conflicted feelings about predation and loss.
counterfactuals.output:
At first light the paddocks loosen their breath—  
blue morning light pooled in the hoofprints,  
a cold glaze on the trough, on the corrugated tin  
of the shed roof ticking like an old throat  
after the night’s heat has gone out of it.

Wattle trees lean over the fence-line,  
their yellow sifted gold too bright for grief,  
each blossom a small sun the world spends freely  
while the creek, lower each year, keeps its counsel  
under reeds, under cow-bones, under clay.

Above the ridge the eagles turn.  
They do not ask permission of beauty.  
They write their hunger in widening rings,  
shadowing the lambs with a patience  
that feels almost like prayer.

I have cursed them from the yards,  
flung my voice like a stone at the sky,  
then stood ashamed beneath that vast, blue law—  
for what is a life here but taking  
and being taken, grass into wool,  
mouse into talon, rain into dust?

Still, when the ewe noses the torn place  
where her lamb has gone quiet,  
the morning falters. The wattles burn on.  
Tin flashes. Flies gather their black scripture.  
And I, with my two human hands,  
want mercy to descend like weather,

want the eagle fed without the lamb’s undoing,  
want the paddock green without the creek’s surrender,  
want loss to be less intimate than this—  
not fleece snagged on wire, not blood in the sedge,  
not the high, clean cry fading eastward  
over a country that keeps making room

for hunger, for blossom, for the blue hour’s  
merciless tenderness: the shed, the trees,  
the circling wings, the earth opening and closing  
its many mouths, and my heart among them,  
half-root, half-claw, learning again  
to love what will not spare us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose-poem with minimal punctuation and enjambed line breaks, in which a narrator returns home, notices a vanished wattle tree, and is emotionally steadied by two huge eagles passing over the roof.
counterfactuals.output:
I come home by the old road  
with dust loosening from my shoes  

the house is smaller than memory  
or memory has grown too full of rooms  

where the wattle stood  
there is only light  
a blunt patch of sky  
and the fence showing through  

no yellow weather  
no bees thick in the noon  
no branch to lean its soft weight  
against the heat  

I stand with my hand on the gate  
as if the latch can explain  
what time has taken  
without sound  

then the roof darkens  

two huge eagles pass over  
slow as lifted gates  
their wings holding the air open  

and something in me  
that had been falling  
finds for a moment  
its wide black shape  

they go on without turning  
beyond the chimney  
beyond the empty place  
where the wattle made gold  

and I breathe  

not healed  
not certain  

only steadied  
by their vastness  
moving above the house  
as if the sky still knows  
how to carry what is gone
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of someone overwhelmed by ecological grief, trying to explain how the sight of two eagles above their house makes the surrounding damage briefly bearable.
counterfactuals.output:
This morning, the creek stank of gasoline,  
and the maples wore their burnt-edged leaves  
like warnings they were tired of giving.

All week I have been counting losses—  
the frogs gone quiet in the ditch,  
the bees like bits of ash on the sill,  
the hot wind worrying the garden  
until even the tomatoes seemed afraid.

I have tried to speak of it plainly,  
but my mouth fills with dead rivers.  
I have tried to be useful—  
called, signed, planted, pleaded—  
and still the hill is thinner each year,  
still the sky coughs, still the rain  
arrives wrong or not at all.

Then above the house, two eagles.

Not symbols. I am too tired for symbols.  
Just bodies: vast, deliberate, alive,  
turning on a column of air I could not see.  
Their wings held open  
as if the world, even damaged,  
could still lift something.

For a moment the landfill beyond the pines  
was only distance.  
The chainsaws down the road  
fell out of hearing.  
Even the grief in me, that dark animal,  
lowered its head.

They circled once, twice—  
black script written on the glare—  
and I stood beneath them  
with my small human sorrow,  
my hands empty, my house behind me,  
the poisoned earth underfoot,

and somehow did not break.

Not because anything was healed.  
The creek was still sick.  
The fields still browned.  
The future still stood there  
with its mouth full of smoke.

But those two eagles stayed in the air  
a little longer than my despair expected,  
and the day, ruined as it was,  
made room for them.

So I made room too.  
I breathed the bitter air.  
I watched until they vanished  
beyond the wounded trees,

and for the length of their leaving,  
I could bear to love the world  
again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary free verse poem about landscape, home, birds of prey, and environmental trauma, ending with the speaker admitting that this is all the sense they can make “in such blue light.”
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of the subdivision  
the field remembers being field  
under the poured slabs, under the cul-de-sacs  
named for trees no longer standing.

My mother calls it progress  
when the new roofs catch the sun.  
I call it a kind of weather  
that arrived with paperwork,  
orange flags, the long-necked machines  
lowering their mouths to the earth.

Home is the place  
I keep returning to incorrectly.

Above the drainage ditch  
a red-tailed hawk turns one slow circle,  
reading the heat that rises  
from asphalt, from shingles,  
from the black pond filmed with oil.

It does not forgive us.  
It does not accuse.  
It only holds itself open  
on the ruined air.

All summer the creek ran shallow,  
then brown, then not at all.  
Fish flashed their last small mirrors  
in the cracked bed.  
The sycamores dropped leaves early  
as if trying to lighten the body  
before impact.

At night I hear owls  
threading the dark with questions  
too old for language.  
They hunt where the meadow was,  
where the mice have learned  
the hard geography of fences.

What is a homeland  
after the soil is hauled off  
in trucks?  
What is grief  
when it comes with receipts,  
permits, a ribbon cutting,  
a model kitchen filled with light?

Still, I set a chair  
by the west window.  
Still, I watch the kestrel  
hover over the road’s bright wound,  
wings shivering, fixed  
to some invisible pressure.

Maybe survival is not hope.  
Maybe it is only attention—  
the hawk’s shadow crossing the lawn,  
the dead pine standing like a witness,  
the smoke-colored hills  
holding their breath beyond us.

I wanted the world  
to explain itself.  
Instead, the evening opens  
its damaged hands,  
and the birds keep circling  
what we have taken.

This is all the sense I can make  
in such blue light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
